contributions.headingText: Lipomatosis is diffuse overgrowth of adipose tissue. Subclassification is based on clinical findings and anatomical distribution.
Diffuse lipomatosis; multiple symmetrical lipomatosis; pelvic lipomatosis; steroid lipomatosis; HIV lipodystrophy

Diffuse lipomatosis involves the trunk, a large portion of an extremity, head and neck, abdomen, pelvis, or intestines. Macrodactyly or gigantism of a digit may be present {1892721; 5770417}. Symmetrical lipomatosis manifests as symmetrical deposition of fat in the upper body, particularly the neck. In pelvic lipomatosis there is diffuse overgrowth of fat in the perivesical and perirectal areas. Steroid lipomatosis is characterized by accumulation of fat in the face, sternal region, or upper-middle back (buffalo hump). HIV lipodystrophy shows accumulation of visceral fat, breast adiposity, and cervical fat pads {9675454; 11746223}.

Patients present with massive accumulation of fat in affected areas that may mimic a neoplasm. Patients with symmetrical lipomatosis can have neuropathy and involvement of the CNS {7783758; 3179687}. Accumulation of fat in the lower neck can cause laryngeal obstruction and compression of the vena cava. Pelvic lipomatosis causes urinary frequency, perineal pain, constipation, and abdominal and back pain. Bowel obstruction and hydronephrosis can develop. Imaging in lipomatosis shows the extent of fat accumulation and excludes other processes. Patients with HIV treated with antiretroviral medications may develop hyperlipidaemia, insulin resistance, and fat wasting in the face and limbs {25598476}.

Lipomatosis is rare. Diffuse lipomatosis usually occurs in children aged < 2 years, but it may affect adults. Pelvic lipomatosis often affects black males aged 9–80 years; the incidence is 0.6–1.7 cases per 100 000 hospital admissions in the USA {30681625}. Multiple symmetrical lipomatosis develops in middle-aged men (M:F ratio: 15:1) of Mediterranean descent, and the incidence is 1 case per 25 000 person-years {22301856}. Patients have a history of liver disease or excessive alcohol consumption. Steroid lipomatosis manifests in patients on hormone therapy or who have increased endogenous production of adrenocortical steroids. Lipodystrophy is seen in HIV-positive patients treated with antiretroviral therapy.

Multiple symmetrical lipomatosis is associated with liver disease or excessive alcohol consumption. Steroid lipomatosis manifests in patients on hormone therapy or who have increased endogenous production of adrenocortical steroids. HIV-infected patients treated with nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors and protease inhibitors often develop lipodystrophy {25598476}.
Patients with multiple symmetrical lipomatosis have mutations in mitochondrial DNA genes; familial subtypes are recognized {30873109; 30283804}.
Grossly, lipomatosis appears as poorly circumscribed, soft, yellow fat identical to normal fat. The differences are the site and distribution of the fat.
All of the different types of lipomatosis have identical morphological features, consisting of lobules and sheets of mature adipocytes that may infiltrate other structures such as skeletal muscle.
Essential: diffuse overgrowth of mature adipose tissue.

Idiopathic forms of lipomatosis tend to recur after surgery. Treatment is palliative surgical removal of excess fat. Massive accumulation of fat in the neck region may cause death due to laryngeal obstruction. Fat in steroid lipomatosis regresses after steroid levels are lowered. Patients with HIV treated with antiretroviral medications may experience metabolic disturbances.
